That is the empire: a princeps, later openly an emperor, over a vast territory of cities, taxes, and law. Roman citizenship spreads, and in 212 CE Caracalla extends it to nearly all free inhabitants. Roman law, built of jurists’ opinions and imperial decrees, becomes the ancestor of the civil-law tradition.

The empire is also slavery, spectacle, crucifixion, and conquest. It is roads, concrete, and a legal idea that a rule can be stated and appealed. In the third century it nearly breaks. Diocletian reorganizes it. Constantine favors Christianity and founds a new capital at Constantinople. Theodosius makes Christianity the empire’s official religion. In 476 a Germanic commander deposes the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus. That date is a marker, not the moment antiquity switches off. The eastern empire continues for a thousand years.

entries.title: Christianity becomes public
paras: Jesus of Nazareth is a Jew in Roman Judea, executed under the prefect Pontius Pilate around 30 CE. His followers say he rose. The movement spreads through synagogues and cities of the empire, and Paul argues that gentiles may join without becoming Jews. For centuries Christians are a minority, sometimes tolerated and sometimes persecuted, with a reputation for refusing the emperor’s cult.

Constantine converts in the fourth century and patronizes the church. Councils, especially Nicaea in 325, define doctrine using the empire’s habit of issuing a decision. By the end of the century Christianity is the official religion. The church then has bishops, wealth, and the problem of what to do with power. Augustine, around 400, writes a theology that will dominate the Latin west, including a bleak account of human will that later reformers rediscover.

entries.title: Islam and the caliphates
paras: Muhammad preaches in Mecca and, in 622, moves to Medina. That move, the Hijra, starts the Islamic calendar. The Quran is received by Muslims as revelation. Within a generation of his death in 632, Arab armies hold Syria, Egypt, Persia, and more. The speed is one of the shocks of history. People in the new empire are not all converted at the point of a sword. Islamization takes centuries. A tax distinction between Muslims and others is part of the early system.

A split over succession becomes the Sunni and Shia traditions. The Umayyads rule from Damascus, the Abbasids from Baghdad. Baghdad in the eighth to tenth centuries is a capital of translation: Greek philosophy and science, Persian statecraft, and Indian mathematics enter Arabic. Ibn Sina and Ibn Rushd, algebra and optics, hospitals and paper are part of that world. The Mongols sack Baghdad in 1258. Islamic civilization does not end. New centers rise in Cairo, Anatolia, Persia, India, and West Africa.

entries.title: Buddhism’s spread
paras: The Buddha teaches in northern India in the fifth century BCE, or thereabouts: suffering has a cause in craving, and a path can loosen it. The teaching splits into schools. Theravada becomes strong in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. Mahayana, with its bodhisattvas, travels the Silk Road into China, Korea, and Japan, and into Tibet in a tantric form.

Buddhism changes as it moves. In China it meets Confucian duty to family and Daoist talk of the way, and it becomes a Chinese religion with monasteries the state sometimes funds and sometimes closes. Ashoka’s patronage in India and later kings in Southeast Asia tie it to politics. It largely fades in the land of its birth as Hindu traditions and, later, Islam reshape India, while remaining a world religion elsewhere.

entries.title: Confucius and the scholar-official
paras: Confucius, in the troubled last centuries of the Zhou, teaches that a good society depends on ritual, filial duty, and rulers who behave as if their example matters. He does not found a church. His sayings, the Analects, are collected by students. Over centuries the tradition becomes the training of Chinese officials: the classics, the exams, the idea that learning qualifies a person to govern.

That ideal is never the whole of Chinese power. Emperors use it, ignore it, and punish scholars. It also travels to Korea, Japan, and Vietnam, each of which adapts it. A person who knows only the European canon should know this one too, because for a very long time more people were governed in its shadow than in Aristotle’s.

entries.title: Byzantium
paras: The eastern Roman empire, which historians call Byzantine, is Roman law, Greek language, and an Orthodox church, ruled from Constantinople. Justinian in the sixth century codifies Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis, the book later Europe will study, and briefly retakes parts of the west. The empire then loses Syria and Egypt to the Arab conquests and survives by tax, diplomacy, Greek fire, and walls.

In 1054 the eastern and western churches formally split, a break that had been growing for centuries. In 1204 crusaders sack Constantinople, a wound the empire does not fully heal. In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II takes the city. Scholars leaving for Italy carry Greek books. Moscow later claims the mantle of a third Rome. The empire had already lasted longer than a person usually remembers.

entries.title: Medieval Europe
paras: After the western empire’s political collapse, power is local: Germanic kingdoms, a Latin church, and a memory of Rome. Charlemagne is crowned emperor in 800 and gathers scholars, then his empire is divided. What later writers call feudalism is a patchwork of personal ties: land granted for military service, lords and vassals, and serfs bound to estates. It is not one neat pyramid, and it is not the same in every valley.

The church is the international institution. Monasteries copy books. Popes and kings fight over who appoints bishops. Universities grow in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries out of cathedral schools. Thomas Aquinas tries to hold Aristotle and Christian doctrine in one system. Gothic cathedrals are the engineering of that confident church. Most people are peasants. Their history is in rents, sermons, and the occasional revolt, not in the chronicles of kings.

entries.title: Magna Carta
paras: In 1215 English barons force King John to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede. It is a peace treaty between a king and his elites, full of feudal grievances. Most of its clauses die with that world. Two ideas do not. In substance, a free man is not to be imprisoned, dispossessed, outlawed, or exiled except by the lawful judgment of his peers or by the law of the land. And right and justice are not to be sold, denied, or delayed.

John gets the pope to annul it. It is reissued anyway, and later parliaments treat it as a statute. In the seventeenth century English opponents of the Stuart kings read it as a charter of liberty far beyond what the barons meant. American revolutionaries inherit that reading. The document is a lesson in how a text can outgrow its authors without becoming a forgery. The words about judgment and the law of the land are the ones to remember.

entries.title: The Crusades
paras: In 1095 Pope Urban II calls knights to aid the eastern Christians and take Jerusalem. The first crusade takes the city in 1099 and kills many of its inhabitants. Crusader states last in the Levant until Acre falls in 1291. There are later crusades, including the fourth, which in 1204 sacks Christian Constantinople instead.

The crusades are a religious war, a younger-son land grab, a pilgrimage, and a disaster for Jews in the Rhineland, who are massacred by some of the armies on the way. They do not permanently hold Jerusalem. They do deepen the split of Latin and Greek Christians and leave a memory both sides still use. Medieval Spain’s long wars between Christian and Muslim kingdoms, the Reconquista, are a related and separate story, ending in 1492 with Granada.

entries.title: The Mongols
paras: In 1206 Temüjin is acclaimed Chinggis Khan. The Mongol empire becomes the largest contiguous land empire in history, breaking the Jin and the Song in China, the Khwarazmian realm in Central Asia, the Abbasid caliphate’s capital, and the armies of Rus and Hungary. The method is speed, terror as a policy, and recruitment of the skilled people of conquered cities.

The empire splits into khanates. In China the Yuan dynasty is Mongol and also a Chinese dynasty. Pax Mongolica, such as it is, makes the Silk Road more passable. The same routes help the plague move. Mongol rule is not only destruction. It is also religious tolerance by imperial indifference, a postal system, and a demonstration that steppe cavalry can still humble settled empires. Timur, later, shows the pattern is not finished.

entries.title: The Black Death
paras: In the middle of the fourteenth century, plague crosses from the Black Sea ports into the Mediterranean and then the rest of Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa. In a few years it kills a huge share of the people in its path. In Europe the common estimate is something like a third to a half. The numbers are not a ledger. Villages disappear. Priests die. People look for someone to blame, and attacks on Jews follow in many towns.

The economic aftershock is as important as the shock. Labor is scarce. Wages rise where workers can bargain. Serfdom weakens in western Europe and, in some eastern lands, landlords tighten it instead. The authority of institutions that could not stop the dying is damaged. Later outbreaks return for centuries. The bacterium is Yersinia pestis, identified long afterward. People at the time had theories, none of them the bacterium, and they acted on those theories.

entries.title: African kingdoms
paras: Africa is not a preface to the slave trade. Aksum, in the Ethiopian highlands, is a trading kingdom and an early Christian state. Ghana, Mali, and Songhai control gold and salt across the Sahara. Mansa Musa of Mali, on a hajj in the fourteenth century, spends so much gold in Cairo that the story reaches Europe and later maps. Timbuktu is a city of trade and of manuscript learning.

Along the east coast, Swahili cities speak an African language and practice Islam, trading with Arabia, Persia, and India. Great Zimbabwe, in the south, is a stone city built by local Shona-speaking people, whatever nineteenth-century Europeans later refused to believe. In the forests of the west, kingdoms such as Benin cast bronze that still corrects anyone who thought technique lived only on the Mediterranean.

entries.title: The Americas before 1492
paras: Maize is domesticated in Mesoamerica and becomes the staff of life from the Andes to the Great Lakes. The Maya city-states of the classic period have writing, a precise calendar, and kings who record wars. The Mexica, or Aztecs, build Tenochtitlan in a lake and rule a tribute empire. Their sacrifice is real and was the horror their enemies remembered. Their markets, law, and canals are also real.

The Inca hold the Andes with roads, storehouses, and a knotted-string record, the quipu, and without a writing system of the Maya kind. In North America, Cahokia near the Mississippi is a city of mounds. The Haudenosaunee, the Iroquois confederacy, bind nations in a league. None of these are waiting to be discovered. They are political worlds. After 1492, disease, animals, and invasion break many of them with a speed that still structures the hemisphere.

entries.title: The Renaissance
paras: Renaissance means rebirth, and the people who used the word meant a rebirth of Greek and Roman letters. It begins in the Italian cities, where merchants have money and the ruins of Rome are local. Petrarch hunts manuscripts. Artists study bodies and perspective. Florence under the Medici is the famous case, not the only one. The movement is a shift in taste and education among elites, not a switch that turns the Middle Ages off.

Printing, patronage, and the fall of Constantinople’s libraries feed it. Northern Europe has its own Renaissance, more religious and more domestic in its art. Machiavelli writes, from the wreck of Italian independence, that a ruler who wishes to keep a state must look at how power actually behaves. That book is still quoted by people who have not read the republican chapters.

entries.title: The printing press
paras: Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz makes a press with movable metal type practical for Europe. Block printing and movable type already exist in East Asia. What changes in Europe is the combination of cheap rag paper, a press, an alphabet of few letters, and a market of readers. A book that took a scribe months can be set and printed in many copies.

The press does not make everyone agree. It makes disagreement cheaper. The Reformation is the first great pamphlet war. Scientific tables and vernacular Bibles travel. So do forgeries and witch-hunting manuals. Authority has to argue in public more often. States learn to license presses. The habit of a private person owning a text is the long result.

entries.title: The Reformation
paras: In 1517 Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar, objects to the sale of indulgences and then to the pope’s claim over the conscience. He translates the Bible into German. The printing press carries him. Rulers who want church lands and less interference from Rome adopt the reform. John Calvin in Geneva builds a stricter Protestant city. Henry VIII of England breaks with Rome over a marriage and keeps a church that is Catholic in much of its look and Protestant in its head.

The wars that follow are about doctrine and about who holds the state. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 lets German princes choose Lutheran or Catholic for their lands. France’s wars of religion, the Dutch revolt against Spain, and the Thirty Years’ War, ended in 1648 at Westphalia, kill on a terrible scale. Westphalia does not invent the modern state by a signature. It does confirm that more than one church will survive inside Europe, and that princes, not the pope, will decide a great deal.

entries.title: Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal empires
paras: Three great Muslim empires shape the early modern world beside Europe, and often more powerfully. The Ottomans take Constantinople in 1453, the Balkans, much of the Arab world, and in 1529 reach the walls of Vienna. Their system includes the devshirme, a levy of Christian boys trained as soldiers and officials, and a law that mixes sultanic decree with Islamic jurisprudence. Suleiman in the sixteenth century is the famous peak.

The Safavids make Iran Shiite, a decision that still marks the map. The Mughals, Timurid princes from Central Asia, rule most of India. Akbar tries a wide religious policy. Shah Jahan builds the Taj Mahal as a tomb. Aurangzeb expands the empire and strains it. These are not a backdrop to Europe. Silver from the Americas reaches them. Their decline, later, is real and is not the same thing as a European plan.

entries.title: 1492 and the Columbian exchange
paras: In 1492 Columbus, sailing for Castile, reaches the Caribbean. He is looking for Asia. He has found a hemisphere that already has tens of millions of people. Spain and Portugal, with a papal line and the Treaty of Tordesillas, claim a division of the non-Christian world. Conquest follows: Cortés against the Aztec empire, Pizarro against the Inca, and a longer, messier takeover of the continents.

Disease does more killing than swords. Populations with no experience of smallpox, measles, and the rest collapse. That catastrophe is the central fact of early American history. The exchange the other way remakes the world too. Maize and potatoes feed Europe, China, and Africa. Silver from Potosí becomes global money. Horses change the plains. Sugar, planted with enslaved labor, becomes the rich commodity. 1492 is a hinge because two worlds that had been apart become one disease pool and one market.

entries.title: The Atlantic slave trade
paras: European colonies in the Americas want labor for mines and, above all, sugar. Indigenous populations have been shattered by disease and are not enough, and in many places the law comes to restrict their enslavement. Traders turn to West and Central Africa. African states and merchants sell captives, often taken in war, to Portuguese, British, French, Dutch, Spanish, and other buyers. About twelve million people are embarked across the Atlantic. A large share die on the voyage or in the first years of a plantation.

This is not an ancient universal slavery with a new route. The scale, the racial law that follows, and the inheritance of status through the mother make a new system. The Middle Passage is the ocean part: packed ships, revolt, and drowning. Enslaved people make cultures anyway, in Brazil, the Caribbean, and North America, and they rebel, most successfully in Haiti. Abolition, when it comes, is late, argued by the enslaved and by religious and political reformers, and resisted because the profits are large.

entries.title: The scientific revolution
paras: In 1543 Copernicus publishes a sun-centered system, and Vesalius publishes a human anatomy drawn from dissection. The change is not that everyone suddenly experiments. It is that a few people decide nature should be described mathematically and checked against the sky and the body, not only against old books. Kepler finds that planets move in ellipses. Galileo sees moons around Jupiter with a telescope and is tried in 1633 for holding the Copernican system as fact. The trial is real. It is not the whole relationship of science and religion, which is also patronage, Jesuit astronomers, and Protestant natural philosophers.

Newton’s Principia in 1687 gives one law of gravitation for the apple and the moon, or so the later story says, and a method: state the rule, derive the consequences, compare them to observation. The Royal Society and similar bodies make experiment a public habit. The result, slowly, is a world in which a claim about nature can be beaten by a measurement. That habit will build industry, medicine, and weapons.

entries.title: England’s revolutions and the Bill of Rights
paras: The English civil wars pit Parliament against Charles I. In 1649 the king is tried and beheaded, a shock in a world of divine-right monarchy. Cromwell’s republic becomes a protectorate, then the monarchy returns in 1660. Charles II and James II reopen the fight over religion and the king’s power to ignore law. In 1688 James flees. Parliament offers the crown to William and Mary on terms.

The Bill of Rights of 1689 is those terms. In substance: the crown cannot suspend laws or levy taxes without Parliament. Elections should be free. Speech in Parliament is not to be questioned in the courts. Excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments are forbidden. A standing army in peacetime needs Parliament’s consent. Protestants may have arms for their defense, as allowed by law. It is a Protestant, parliamentary settlement, not a universal declaration. American lawyers will copy several of its phrases almost exactly.

entries.title: The Enlightenment
paras: The Enlightenment is a set of arguments, mostly in the eighteenth century, that reason, evidence, and criticism can reform belief, law, and government. Locke says government rests on consent and that people have rights it may not casually take. Montesquieu says power should be divided. Voltaire attacks cruelty and clerical power. The Encyclopédie tries to collect the arts and sciences. Kant tells the reader to think without a guardian.

It is not a single party, and it is not innocent. Many of its writers accept empire. Some accept slavery while writing about liberty, and some, like the later abolitionists who use their language, do not. Mary Wollstonecraft applies the same rights talk to women and is told the culture is not ready. The Enlightenment’s tool is the one this shelf uses: a public argument that a reader can answer. Its danger is the belief that a reasonable person has already finished thinking.

entries.title: The American Revolution
paras: After the Seven Years’ War, Britain tries to tax and regulate its American colonies more closely. Colonists who have been governing themselves in assemblies answer that taxation without their consent is illegal. Protest, boycott, and violence follow. In 1776 the Continental Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence. The war is not a skirmish. It takes French money, a French fleet, and a French army, and it ends with British surrender at Yorktown in 1781 and a treaty in 1783.

The revolution is about self-government, and it is led in large part by men who hold slaves. That contradiction is not a modern discovery. People at the time, including some of the enslaved who flee to the British lines, say it. The new states write constitutions. The first national frame, the Articles of Confederation, makes a league too weak to tax or to hold a common trade policy. That failure is why a convention meets in 1787.

entries.title: How the Constitution was argued
paras: The Philadelphia convention of 1787 is called to revise the Articles. It writes a new frame instead and sends it to state conventions. The design is a compromise at every joint. Large states and small states split Congress into a House by population and a Senate by states. Slave states want enslaved people counted for representation. The three-fifths clause counts them as three-fifths for seats and taxes, and it does not give them votes. The slave trade is protected from a federal ban until 1808. These are political bargains, written down. They are in the text on this shelf.

Federalists, including Hamilton, Madison, and Jay in the Federalist papers, argue that a large republic can control faction better than a small one, and that ambition can be made to counteract ambition if the branches are separate. Anti-Federalists answer that the new government is too strong, too distant, and has no bill of rights. Ratification is close in several states. The promise of amendments produces the Bill of Rights in 1791. Madison’s own fear, in Federalist 10, is that a majority will use the state against a minority. The Constitution’s later history is in large part the fight over who counts as part of the people.

entries.title: The French Revolution and Napoleon
paras: In 1789 a financial crisis forces Louis XVI to call the Estates-General. The Third Estate declares itself a national assembly. A crowd storms the Bastille. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen says men are born free and equal in rights, that sovereignty sits in the nation, and that liberty is doing what does not harm others. The declaration is a program and a weapon. The king tries to flee. War begins. In 1793 the king is executed and the revolution turns to terror, executing its enemies and then its friends in the name of public safety.

Napoleon Bonaparte takes the state in 1799 and crowns himself emperor in 1804. He exports the revolution’s law and its conscription. The Napoleonic Code sweeps away feudal privilege and confirms paternal power and a limited place for women. His armies redraw Germany, abolish the Holy Roman Empire, and provoke the nationalism that will oppose him. He is beaten in Russia in 1812 and at Waterloo in 1815. The old kings come back, and they cannot put the idea of the nation back in the bottle.

entries.title: The Haitian Revolution
paras: Saint-Domingue, the French colony on Hispaniola, is the richest sugar colony in the world and one of the most brutal. In 1791 enslaved people rise. The fighting draws in free people of color, French republicans, Spain, and Britain. Toussaint Louverture builds an army and a government. Napoleon sends an expedition to restore slavery. It fails, with disease and resistance both doing the work. In 1804 Haiti declares independence, the first state founded by formerly enslaved people who defeated an empire.

The world of slaveholders is terrified and isolates Haiti. France later demands an indemnity for the lost 'property,' a debt that burdens the country for generations. Haiti’s revolution is the proof that the language of liberty in Paris could be taken up by the people that language had excluded, and that the people who wrote it would often try to take it back.

entries.title: Latin American independence
paras: Spain’s American empires break while Spain is occupied by Napoleon. Creole elites, people of Spanish descent born in America, want office and trade that Madrid had guarded. From 1810, wars of independence run across the continent. Simón Bolívar in the north and José de San Martín from the south are the names schoolbooks keep. Mexico’s path includes a popular rising led by the priest Hidalgo and, later, a more conservative independence under Iturbide. Brazil leaves Portugal in 1822 as an empire under Pedro, without the same kind of war.

Independence does not free the enslaved everywhere at once, and it does not include indigenous nations as equal founders. The new republics inherit borders, the Catholic Church, and armies that often become the real constitution. The nineteenth century in Latin America is independence, civil war, and the argument over what a republic owes the people who are not the creole elite.

entries.title: The industrial revolution
paras: It begins in Britain, where coal, iron, colonies, capital, and a state that enforces property sit together. Machines spin cotton. Steam engines pump mines and then move looms, ships, and trains. Factories gather workers who no longer own their tools. Cities grow faster than drains. A person can see the change in smoke, in the clock at the factory gate, and in the price of cloth.

The early decades are hard on the people inside the mills, including children, and real wages do rise later. That argument, misery then improvement, is the historians’ fight, and both halves have evidence. Other countries follow: Belgium, France, the German states, the United States, and, later and faster, Japan. Industry makes a new kind of power. A state with coal, steel, and rails can feed a mass army. It also makes a new kind of politics, because the people in the mills can organize.

entries.title: Liberalism, nationalism, socialism
paras: The nineteenth century names its arguments. Liberalism, in that century’s sense, means constitutions, parliaments, free speech, and free trade, and it often does not mean democracy. Many liberals fear the poor’s vote. Nationalism says a people who share language, history, or will should have a state. It unifies Germany and Italy and pulls empires apart. It also teaches people to die for a flag.

Socialism says the new industry has made owners rich by using workers who do not own the machines, and that this should be changed, by reform or by revolution. Marx and Engels in 1848 call on the workers of the world to unite. Trade unions, often illegal at first, are the practical version millions of people actually join. Conservatism, the fourth name, says rapid change destroys the institutions that make a society livable. A person should be able to state each of these without a sneer, because each of them is still in the room.

In 1848 revolutions break out across Europe: France, the German states, the Italian states, the Austrian empire, and others. Liberals want constitutions. Nationalists want nations. Workers want bread and the vote. For a season the old order shakes. Then armies, and the splits among the revolutionaries, put most of it back. In France the Second Republic becomes the empire of Napoleon III.

The year matters because the demands do not go home. Parliaments spread. Serfdom ends in the Austrian lands and, in 1861, in Russia. National unification is achieved from above, by Piedmont and by Prussia, as much as from the barricade. 1848 is the rehearsal. The twentieth century will play the piece louder.

entries.title: Abolition
paras: Britain abolishes the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in the 1830s, after revolt in the colonies and a long public campaign at home. The United States bans the import of enslaved people after 1808, as the Constitution had allowed, and keeps a huge internal trade. Slavery expands into new cotton land. Abolitionists, Black and white, are a minority until the war. France abolishes slavery in 1794, restores it under Napoleon, and abolishes it again in 1848. Brazil, the last large slave society in the Americas, abolishes it in 1888.

Abolition is not the same as equality. Former owners are often compensated. Formerly enslaved people often are not given land. The systems built to replace slavery — apprenticeship, sharecropping, vagrancy laws, convict labor — keep the work and change the name. Knowing the date of abolition without knowing what came next is only half the fact.

entries.title: The American Civil War
paras: The United States breaks over slavery’s expansion. The Republican Party’s rise, and Lincoln’s election in 1860 without carrying the deep South, leads eleven states to secede. Their own declarations name slavery as the cause. The Confederacy fights to become a separate country. The Union fights first to restore itself. The war becomes a war against slavery as enslaved people flee to Union lines and as Lincoln issues the Emancipation Proclamation on 1 January 1863, freeing people in the states in rebellion as a war measure.

More than 600,000 soldiers die. The South’s armies surrender in the spring of 1865. Lincoln is murdered. The Thirteenth Amendment abolishes slavery. The war settles that the Union is a nation and that slavery will not be its law. It does not settle what freedom will mean. That fight is Reconstruction, and it is not won in 1865.

entries.title: Reconstruction and its overthrow
paras: After the war, the United States tries to define freedom. The Fourteenth Amendment makes anyone born in the country a citizen and forbids states to deny equal protection or due process. The Fifteenth says the vote shall not be denied on account of race. Black men vote and hold office across the South. Schools are built. It is a radical moment in American law, and the amendments are on this shelf in their own words.

White supremacist violence, the Ku Klux Klan and its cousins, and the fatigue of the North overthrow the experiment. By 1877 the last federal troops leave the political bargain that ends the period. Jim Crow laws, poll taxes, literacy tests, and the Supreme Court’s decision in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 build a segregated order that will last into the 1960s. The amendments remain in the Constitution, partly unenforced, which is why the civil rights movement can demand that the country obey its own text.

entries.title: Expansion and indigenous nations
paras: The United States grows by purchase, war, and settlement: Louisiana from France, Florida from Spain, the north of Mexico by war in the 1840s, Oregon by treaty with Britain. Settlers treat the land as empty. It is not. Indigenous nations are removed, by the Indian Removal Act and the Trail of Tears, by treaty that is broken, and by war. The reservation system and the boarding schools that follow try to end nations as nations and children as members of them.

This is the same century as emancipation. A person can hold both facts. The republic expands freedom for some by taking a continent from others. Later law, including the twentieth century’s slow turn toward tribal sovereignty, does not undo the taking. It is the argument that follows it.

entries.title: Empire in the nineteenth century
paras: Industrial states take empires at a new scale. Britain rules India through a company and then, after 1857, through the crown. The Opium Wars force China to accept opium and treaty ports. France takes Indochina and much of West and North Africa. In the 1880s the Scramble for Africa draws borders in European capitals. The Berlin Conference is the symbol. Resistance is constant and usually outgunned. Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa in 1896 and stays independent. Liberia and, for a long time, Siam also stay outside formal rule.

Empire is not only flags. It is taxes, railways, missionaries, languages of administration, and the idea, stated openly at the time, that some peoples are fit to rule others. The wealth moves. So do the resentments that will fuel the twentieth century’s independence movements. A map of Africa with straight lines is a map of that conference table.

entries.title: Meiji Japan and a changing China
paras: In the 1850s American ships force Japan, which had tightly limited foreign trade, to open ports. The Tokugawa shogunate falls. The Meiji restoration of 1868 puts the emperor at the head of a state that then borrows what it needs: a constitution, a conscript army, industry, and an empire of its own. Japan defeats China in 1895 and Russia in 1905. A non-European power beating a European empire is noticed everywhere under colonial rule.

China in the same years is humiliated by the Opium Wars, the Taiping civil war, and the Boxer crisis. The Qing dynasty falls in 1911. A republic is declared. It does not yet hold the country. The contrast of Meiji Japan and late Qing China is one of the lessons nationalists across Asia draw, sometimes too neatly: reform the state or be partitioned.

entries.title: Why the First World War began
paras: By 1914 Europe is armed, allied, and imperial. Germany, unified and industrial, fears encirclement by France and Russia. France wants Alsace-Lorraine back. Russia presents itself as the protector of Slavs. Austria-Hungary is a multiethnic empire afraid of nationalism, especially in the Balkans. Britain has a naval race with Germany and a small army it can send to France. Plans for mobilization are built so that starting is easier than stopping.

On 28 June 1914 a Serbian nationalist kills the heir to the Austrian throne in Sarajevo. Austria, backed by Germany, makes demands on Serbia. Russia backs Serbia. Mobilization timetables turn a Balkan crisis into a continental war in weeks. The deeper causes are the alliances, the empires, the arms, and the belief in each capital that this war will be short and that waiting is more dangerous than marching. They are wrong about the length.

entries.title: The First World War and the peace
paras: The war is industrial. Machine guns, artillery, gas, and mud make the western front a killing ground where offensives gain yards. The eastern front moves more and destroys empires. The Ottoman empire commits genocide against the Armenians. The United States enters in 1917. Russia leaves after revolution. In 1918 Germany asks for an armistice. About twenty million people are dead, soldiers and civilians.

The Treaty of Versailles and its companions punish Germany, redraw eastern Europe into nations, and hand former Ottoman and German colonies to the victors as mandates, which is empire under a new name. The League of Nations is founded and the United States does not join. Germans are told, by the people who will later lead them into the next war, that the army was not beaten but betrayed. That story is false, and it is politically powerful. The peace settles less than it thinks.

entries.title: The Russian revolutions
paras: In 1917 the Russian empire, exhausted by war and misrule, overthrows the tsar in February. A provisional government tries to continue the war and loses the streets. In October the Bolsheviks, a disciplined socialist party led by Lenin, seize power in the name of the soviets, the workers’ and soldiers’ councils. They make peace with Germany, and they start a civil war.

The Bolsheviks win the civil war and build a one-party state. Stalin, after Lenin, industrializes by force, collectivizes the peasants, and runs a famine in Ukraine and elsewhere and a terror that fills camps. The Soviet Union will be the other superpower of the twentieth century, the patron of revolutions, and a warning about what a party that owns the truth will do with a police. 1917 splits the socialist tradition into social democrats and communists, and that split shapes every later left.

entries.title: The Great Depression
paras: In 1929 the American stock market crashes after a decade of speculation and unequal boom. Banks fail. Unemployment in industrial countries reaches levels that break ordinary politics. World trade shrinks as each country tries to save itself with tariffs. Farmers who had fed the war go broke. In Germany, already paying reparations and already humiliated, the depression makes a democracy look helpless.

Governments answer differently. The American New Deal uses public work, bank reform, and relief, and it does not end the slump by itself. Rearmament and the next war do more of that. The political result of mass unemployment is the lesson: people who cannot feed a family will listen to someone who says the system is a fraud and who names an enemy. Democracies that survive the decade are the ones that keep a minimum of loyalty from people in trouble.

entries.title: Fascism and Nazism
paras: Fascism, named in Italy by Mussolini after 1922, is a politics of nation, leader, and violence against liberals, socialists, and unions. It promises order and empire. Nazism in Germany adds a biological racism at the center. Hitler takes office in 1933 and within months has a dictatorship: other parties banned, camps opened, and Jews excluded from citizenship by the Nuremberg laws of 1935. The regime is popular with many and terror for the rest.

A person should be able to tell fascism from ordinary conservatism and from communism. It is not a free market with flags, and it is not the Soviet system. It glorifies the nation as a body that must be purified, treats violence as proof of seriousness, and puts a leader above law. The democracies spend the 1930s hoping it can be appeased. Germany remilitarizes, takes Austria and Czechoslovakia, and in 1939 attacks Poland.

entries.title: The Second World War
paras: The war in Asia begins earlier than 1939. Japan seizes Manchuria in 1931 and invades China in 1937. In Europe, Germany and the Soviet Union divide Poland. In 1940 France falls. Britain holds. In 1941 Germany invades the Soviet Union, and Japan attacks the United States at Pearl Harbor and sweeps through Southeast Asia. The war is then global. The turning points usually named are Midway and Guadalcanal at sea, El Alamein and Stalingrad on land, and the long Soviet advance from the east.

The Allies are an argument that holds together long enough: Britain, the United States, the Soviet Union, China, and the governments in exile and the resistance. Germany surrenders in May 1945. The United States drops atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August, and Japan surrenders. The dead are on the order of seventy million or more, most of them civilians, including the genocide in Europe and famine and massacre in Asia. The war ends the European claim to rule the world as a right, even though empires try to go back to their colonies.

entries.title: The Holocaust
paras: Nazi Germany murders about six million Jews: by shooting squads in the east, by starvation in ghettos, and by gas in camps built for the purpose, Auschwitz the most famous. This is a state project, planned, staffed, and recorded. It also murders Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, and political enemies in great numbers. The word Holocaust is most often kept for the Jewish genocide. The wider killing is part of the same regime.

Neighbors participate, resist, or look away, and the proportions differ by place. A few countries and many individuals protect people. Most of the murdered never have that chance. After the war the Nuremberg trials state that following orders is not an absolute defense, and the phrase crimes against humanity enters ordinary speech. Memory of the Holocaust becomes a test of whether a society will tell the truth about what it did. Denial is not a historical position. It is a refusal of the records.

entries.title: The bomb and the United Nations
paras: The atomic bomb is a new kind of weapon: one plane, one city. Hiroshima and Nagasaki are the only wartime uses. The people who build it, and the people who order it, know they are crossing a line, and they do it to end the war against Japan and to be first. Within a few years the Soviet Union has the bomb too. The rest of the century is lived inside that fact. Deterrence is the theory that each side’s ability to destroy the other will keep either from starting. It is not a comfort. It is a gamble that holds.

The United Nations is founded in 1945 to replace the League, with a General Assembly of all members and a Security Council in which the victors — the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France, and China — have a veto. It is a club of states, not a world government. It keeps a place where enemies still talk, runs refugees and health, and cannot stop a great power that is determined. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948 lists rights the members say people have. Enforcement is the part they do not agree on.

entries.title: The Cold War
paras: After 1945 the wartime alliance splits. The Soviet Union keeps control of eastern Europe. The United States builds alliances, the Marshall Plan, and a policy called containment. Germany is divided. In 1949 China becomes communist and the Soviets test a bomb. The Korean War, 1950 to 1953, is a hot war inside the cold one. The Cuban missile crisis in 1962 is the nearest approach to nuclear war, ended by a bargain.

The Cold War is fought in Vietnam, in Afghanistan, in coups and counter-coups in Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East, and in a race of rockets and wheat. It is also a competition of ideas: liberal capitalism against party socialism, each claiming to be the side of the future, each supporting dictators when it is convenient. The non-aligned movement is the countries that refuse the choice. The Soviet system ends not by invasion but by its own stall: reform under Gorbachev, revolutions in eastern Europe in 1989, and the dissolution of the Union in 1991.

entries.title: China from empire to reform
paras: The Qing fall in 1911. The republic that follows is weak, warlord-ridden, and then at war with Japan. The Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek and the Communists under Mao Zedong fight each other and, for a time, the Japanese. In 1949 the Communists win. Mao’s China is a party state that redistributes land, attacks old elites, and then, in the Great Leap Forward of the late 1950s, tries to industrialize by will. The result is a famine that kills tens of millions.

The Cultural Revolution, from 1966, turns students against teachers, officials, and parents in the name of permanent revolution, and wrecks a generation’s schooling. After Mao’s death, Deng Xiaoping from 1978 opens the economy to markets and foreign trade while keeping the party’s monopoly of power. China’s rise in the late twentieth century is that bargain: getting rich is allowed, organized opposition is not. A person who remembers only the economic miracle has missed the famine and the bargain.

entries.title: Decolonization
paras: Empires do not give up because they have read a pamphlet. They give up because occupation has become expensive, because colonial soldiers have seen the empires beaten in the world war, and because national movements make the cost higher. India and Pakistan become independent in 1947, in a partition that kills and displaces millions. Indonesia, Vietnam, Algeria, Kenya, Ghana, and dozens of others follow by negotiation or by war. Algeria’s war against France and Vietnam’s wars against France and then the United States are the bitter end of the idea that a European army can stay.

New states inherit borders drawn in Europe, export economies, and elites trained in the colonizer’s language. Some become democracies. Many become one-party states or military regimes, courted by both sides of the Cold War. Independence is real. It is not the end of poverty or of outside power. It is the end of the open claim that foreigners have a right to rule.

entries.title: The American civil rights movement
paras: Segregation in the American South is law, backed by violence. In 1954 the Supreme Court in Brown v. Board of Education says segregated schools are unconstitutional. The people who make that paper real are the ones who walk. The Montgomery bus boycott, the student sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, and the Birmingham campaign force a national audience to look. In 1963 a march on Washington demands jobs and freedom. In 1964 the Civil Rights Act bans discrimination in public places and employment. In 1965, after Selma, the Voting Rights Act puts the federal government behind the Fifteenth Amendment.

The movement is not one leader and not only the South. It argues with itself about nonviolence, Black power, and the North’s quieter segregation. Leaders are killed, including Medgar Evers, Malcolm X, and Martin Luther King Jr. The laws pass and do not finish the work. They do end the open legal caste system of Jim Crow, which had looked permanent to the people who built it.

entries.title: After 1989
paras: In 1989 eastern Europe leaves communist rule, mostly without a war between the blocs. Germany reunifies. The Soviet Union dissolves in 1991. Nelson Mandela is released in 1990, and in 1994 South Africa holds the election that ends apartheid. The European Union deepens. China’s economy grows on the bargain described above. The internet moves from a research network to the place where argument, trade, and surveillance all live.

The attacks of 11 September 2001 by al-Qaeda lead the United States into wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, one of them on a claim about weapons that are not found. A financial crisis in 2008, born in housing debt and the banks that packaged it, throws millions out of work and out of houses. A pandemic of a new coronavirus in 2020 stops ordinary life across the world. None of these is 'the end of history.' They are the reminder that the shelf does not close.

entries.title: Republic, democracy, and rights
paras: A democracy, in the Greek sense, is rule by the people, and in the modern sense it usually means that adults vote and can replace the government. A republic is a state in which the law, not a king’s person, is said to be sovereign. The American founders fear a pure democracy of the moment and build a republic with representation, separated powers, and rights the majority is not supposed to vote away. Later amendments make the democracy wider than the founders did.

Rights in this tradition are claims a person can make against the state and, sometimes, against other people: speech, worship, a fair trial, the vote, equal protection. They are written because experience says majorities and kings both abuse power. A right that is only in a speech is a wish. A right that is in a court, with a lawyer and a record, is a tool. The documents on this shelf are the tools this country actually adopted.

entries.title: Common law, civil law, and judicial review
paras: Two great legal traditions shape the modern world. Common law, from England, grows by decisions of judges, case by case, with juries and a strong role for argument in court. Civil law, from Roman law through the Napoleonic Code, starts from a written code the legislature adopts, and the judge’s job is to apply it. Most countries use one, modified by the other. Religious law, in several traditions, remains a third source, sometimes personal and sometimes the law of the state.

Judicial review is the practice, strongest in the United States since Marbury v. Madison in 1803, by which a court can say a statute violates the constitution and refuse to apply it. It makes a constitution more than a slogan, and it puts a few judges over elected laws. Countries argue about whether that is a safeguard or a usurpation. Both sides are describing the same machine.

entries.title: Economics a citizen should recognize
paras: This is not advice about money. It is a map of words. A market is people trading, with prices signaling scarcity. A monopoly is one seller, and it charges more. Inflation is a general rise in prices, often from too much money chasing goods, or from a shock to supply. A recession is a shrink in the economy. Unemployment is people who want work and cannot find it. A central bank, in the United States the Federal Reserve, tries to keep prices stable and employment high by the supply of money and the cost of credit. It fails sometimes.

Taxes are how a state takes a share. Public debt is how it spends now and pays later. Comparative advantage is the idea that two sides can both gain from trade if each sells what it produces at lower opportunity cost. It does not say that no one is hurt. Capitalism is private ownership of the machines and the right to the profit. Socialism, in its public sense, is social ownership or heavy direction of them. Every real country is a mix. Anyone selling you a pure one is selling a poster.

entries.title: Science that changed daily life
paras: Germ theory, argued by Pasteur, Koch, and others in the nineteenth century, says particular microbes cause particular diseases. That one idea builds sewers, vaccines, antiseptic surgery, and the habit of washing. Anesthesia makes surgery something a person can survive awake-pain. Antibiotics, from the mid-twentieth century, make infections that used to kill into illnesses a drug can end, until overuse breeds resistance.

Electricity, from Faraday’s experiments to Edison and Tesla’s systems, rewires the day. The second industrial revolution is steel, chemicals, oil, and the electric motor. Public health, more than any hero, is why children in many countries now live: clean water, vaccines, and food. A person who thanks only doctors has missed the pipes.

entries.title: Evolution, relativity, DNA, and computing
paras: Darwin and Wallace in the mid-nineteenth century argue that species change by natural selection: variations that help an organism leave offspring become common. The evidence since, from fossils to genomes, has deepened that, not replaced it. It removes the need for a separate act of creation for each species. It does not, by itself, tell a person how to treat a neighbor. People who use it to rank human groups are doing politics, and the biology does not support them.

Einstein’s relativity rewrites gravity and shows that mass and energy are convertible, which is the physics under the bomb and under the sun. Quantum mechanics, built by a generation of physicists, describes the small scale and makes transistors possible. The structure of DNA, set out in 1953, shows how living things copy instructions. Computing, from wartime machines to the personal computer and the network, puts a programmable engine in ordinary hands. Each of these is a tool. Each of them can be used to cure or to watch or to kill. The history of science is not a straight road to wisdom. It is a gain in power.

entries.title: Rulers and founders
paras: Cyrus the Great, sixth century BCE, builds the Persian empire and leaves a reputation, partly his own advertising, for restoring peoples he had conquered.

Pericles leads Athens at its most democratic and most imperial in the fifth century BCE. The funeral speech Thucydides gives him is the classic praise of a city that runs itself, spoken over the dead of a war that city chose.
Ashoka, after a slaughter in Kalinga, has edicts carved that urge restraint. He is the rare conqueror whose own stones say he regrets the conquering.
Augustus ends the Roman civil wars and builds the empire while claiming to restore the republic. The month of August is still his.
Constantine makes Christianity a favored religion of the Roman empire and founds Constantinople, the city that will be the eastern capital for a thousand years.
The Prophet Muhammad founds a community at Medina in 622 that becomes a world religion and, quickly, an empire. Muslims date their calendar from that move.
Charlemagne is crowned emperor in 800 and is remembered as the man who briefly gave western Europe one ruler and a revival of letters.
Suleiman the Magnificent rules the Ottoman empire at its widest in the sixteenth century, a lawgiver as well as a general, while Europe is tearing itself over the Reformation.
Elizabeth I holds England through religious settlement and the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588, and becomes the image of a queen who did not marry the state away.
George Washington commands the Continental Army, presides over the convention that writes the Constitution, serves two terms, and goes home. The going home is the part that astonished contemporaries.
Napoleon exports the French Revolution’s law across Europe at the point of a conscript army and is defeated by the coalition and the Russian winter.

Abraham Lincoln holds the Union together, issues the Emancipation Proclamation, and is killed just as the war ends. The Gettysburg Address is his short argument for why the war had to mean a new birth of freedom.

Gandhi leads Indian mass noncooperation against British rule and is murdered in 1948 by a fellow Hindu who thinks he concedes too much to Muslims. Nonviolence, in his hands, is a tactic of pressure, not a mood.

Mandela leaves prison in 1990 after twenty-seven years and leads South Africa into a nonracial election in 1994. The fact people use him for is that he did not answer a long imprisonment with a civil war.

entries.title: Thinkers, scientists, and witnesses
paras: Confucius teaches that rulers and families are held together by ritual and example. East Asian states will train officials on his tradition for two millennia.
Aristotle, a student of Plato and a teacher of Alexander, writes the books on logic, politics, and nature that medieval Islam and medieval Europe will both call simply the Philosopher.
Ibn Sina, Avicenna, around the year 1000, writes a canon of medicine used from Persia to Europe for centuries, a product of the translation culture of the Islamic world.
Thomas Aquinas, in the thirteenth century, tries to show that Christian doctrine and Aristotelian reason do not have to be enemies. Universities grow up around that kind of argument.
Martin Luther starts the Protestant Reformation and puts a Bible in German into lay hands. He also writes against the Jews in terms later persecutors will use. Both are his.

John Locke argues that government is a trust, that people may replace it, and that the mind is furnished by experience. The Declaration of Independence is downstream of him, slavery and all: Locke invested in the trade.
Mary Wollstonecraft, in 1792, writes that the rights of man are an unfinished sentence if they leave women ornamental and uneducated.

Marx, with Engels, describes industrial capitalism as a system that produces its own gravediggers. However a person judges the revolutions done in his name, the description of the factory is one of the nineteenth century’s unavoidable books.
Charles Darwin gives biology a mechanism, natural selection, that does not need a separate creation for each species.
Marie Curie isolates radioactive elements and wins two Nobel prizes, and dies of the radiation she studied. She is the clean example of a science that costs the scientist.
Einstein rewrites space, time, and energy. His letter to Roosevelt about a possible German bomb is part of why the American bomb project starts. He later warns about the world he helped arm.

W. E. B. Du Bois, a historian and a founder of the NAACP, writes across seven decades that the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color line, and he documents it instead of only denouncing it.

entries.title: Dates worth being able to place
paras: About 3000 BCE. Cities and writing are established in Mesopotamia and Egypt.
About 1750 BCE. Hammurabi’s code is inscribed in Babylon.
About 1250 BCE. A traditional date for the late Bronze Age crises that topple several eastern Mediterranean kingdoms.
563 to 483 BCE, traditionally. The Buddha’s lifetime. Confucius is his near contemporary, 551 to 479 BCE.
490 and 480 BCE. Greek cities defeat Persian invasions at Marathon and then at Salamis and Plataea.
323 BCE. Alexander dies in Babylon. His generals divide the empire.
27 BCE. Augustus becomes the first Roman emperor in practice.
About 30 CE. Jesus is executed under Roman authority in Judea.
212 CE. Roman citizenship is extended to nearly all free people in the empire.
325. The Council of Nicaea defines a creed for Christianity.
476. The last western Roman emperor in Italy is deposed. The eastern empire continues.
622. The Hijra, Muhammad’s move to Medina, year one of the Islamic calendar.
800. Charlemagne is crowned emperor in Rome.
1054. The eastern and western Christian churches formally split.
1066. The Norman conquest of England.
1095. Pope Urban II calls the First Crusade.
1215. Magna Carta is sealed at Runnymede.
1258. The Mongols sack Baghdad.
1347. Plague enters the Mediterranean world. The Black Death follows.
1453. The Ottomans take Constantinople.
About 1450. Gutenberg’s press is working in Mainz.
1492. Columbus reaches the Caribbean. Granada falls. Jews are expelled from Spain.
1517. Luther’s protest begins the Reformation in earnest.
1521 and 1533. The Aztec and then the Inca empires fall to Spanish-led conquest.
1588. The Spanish Armada fails against England.
1648. The Peace of Westphalia closes the Thirty Years’ War.
1687. Newton publishes the Principia.
1689. The English Bill of Rights.
1776. The Declaration of Independence.
1787. The United States Constitution is written. It is ratified the next year.
1789. The French Revolution begins. The Declaration of the Rights of Man is adopted.
1791. The American Bill of Rights is ratified. The Haitian Revolution begins.
1804. Haiti declares independence. Napoleon crowns himself.
1807. Britain abolishes the Atlantic slave trade.
1815. Waterloo. Napoleon’s wars end.
1848. Revolutions across Europe. Marx and Engels publish the Communist Manifesto.
1857. The Indian rebellion. Britain then rules India directly.
1861 to 1865. The American Civil War. The Emancipation Proclamation is 1 January 1863.
1868. The Meiji restoration in Japan. The Fourteenth Amendment is ratified in the United States.
1884 to 1885. The Berlin Conference partitions Africa on paper.
1911. The Qing dynasty falls.
1914 to 1918. The First World War.
1917. The Russian revolutions. The United States enters the world war.
1929. The crash that opens the Great Depression.
1933. Hitler takes power in Germany.
1937. Japan’s full invasion of China.
1939 to 1945. The Second World War in Europe. The Holocaust is carried out. Atomic bombs are dropped in August 1945.
1947. India and Pakistan become independent. The Cold War is already underway.
1948. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Israel is established. Gandhi is killed.
1949. The Chinese Communist revolution wins. NATO is founded.
1954. Brown v. Board of Education.
1962. The Cuban missile crisis.
1964 and 1965. The Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act.
1978. Deng Xiaoping’s reforms begin in China.
1989. Eastern Europe leaves communist rule. The Berlin Wall opens.
1991. The Soviet Union dissolves.
1994. South Africa’s first nonracial election. Rwanda’s genocide.
2001. The attacks of September 11. The war in Afghanistan begins.
2008. A global financial crisis.
2020. A coronavirus pandemic shuts ordinary life across the world.
